questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of backward vertical integration?
options: Combining with a supplier, moving back down the supply chain
Combining with a customer or distributor
Combining with a competitor at the same stage
Combining with a business in an unrelated industry
questions.why: Backward means towards the supplier. It secures supply, controls input cost and quality, and reduces supplier power.

questions.stem: A supermarket buys a farm that supplies it. This is:
options: backward vertical integration
forward vertical integration
horizontal integration
conglomerate integration
questions.why: The farm is a supplier, so the supermarket has moved back down its own supply chain.
whyNot: Forward would mean buying something closer to the final customer.
Horizontal would mean buying another supermarket.
Conglomerate would mean an unrelated industry.

questions.stem: Two airlines of similar size agree to combine. This is:
options: horizontal integration
backward vertical integration
forward vertical integration
conglomerate integration
questions.why: Same industry, same stage. Horizontal deals bring market share and economies of scale, and are the most likely to attract competition authority scrutiny.
whyNot: Neither is a supplier to the other.
Neither is a distributor for the other.
Airlines are the same industry, not unrelated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of synergy?
options: The idea that two combined businesses are worth more than the sum of their parts
The premium paid above the market value of a target
The process of investigating a business before buying it
A takeover opposed by the target's board
questions.why: Synergy is the justification for most acquisitions, usually through cost savings or cross-selling. It is promised before a deal and often not delivered after it.

questions.stem: What is the most common reason acquisitions fail to create value for the acquirer?
options: Overpayment, because the premium exceeds the synergies achieved
The target business always collapses
Competition authorities always block them
Acquisitions are illegal in most countries
questions.why: Buying control requires a premium, and the promised synergies frequently fall short of it. Overpayment and culture clash are the two standard causes of failure.
whyNot: Targets usually continue trading; the problem is the price paid.
Most deals proceed; only some face intervention.

questions.stem: Why is culture clash such a common cause of acquisition failure?
options: Two workforces with different ways of working do not merge because a contract was signed
Cultures are legally required to remain separate
Culture has no effect on business performance
Staff always welcome acquisitions
questions.why: Different pay structures, working practices and loyalties persist long after the deal. Integration failure is more common than financial failure, which is why examiners look for this point.
whyNot: It affects motivation, retention and productivity directly.
Acquisitions typically create anxiety about job security.

questions.stem: What is the main criticism of conglomerate diversification?
options: There is no synergy, and shareholders could diversify their own portfolios more cheaply
It is illegal in most countries
It always reduces total revenue
It concentrates risk in one market
questions.why: No shared costs, no shared customers and no management expertise in the new industry. Investors can spread their own risk by buying different shares, so the company adds little by doing it for them.
whyNot: It usually raises revenue by adding a business.
It spreads risk, which is its main justification.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of due diligence?
options: Detailed investigation of a business before acquiring it, to verify finances and identify risks
The premium paid to gain control of a target
The legal process of registering a merger
The integration of two workforces after a deal
questions.why: Due diligence is what should find hidden liabilities before the deal completes. It does not always succeed, which is one of the financial risks of acquisition.

questions.stem: Why does a debt-funded acquisition increase risk?
options: Gearing and interest costs rise, reducing resilience if trading worsens
Debt never has to be repaid
Debt dilutes ownership
Interest payments are optional
questions.why: The interest must be paid whether or not the synergies materialise. A highly geared acquirer facing a downturn has very little room to manoeuvre.
whyNot: It must be repaid with interest.
Debt preserves ownership; equity dilutes it.

questions.stem: What should always be compared against an acquisition proposal?
options: The organic alternative, and whether speed is genuinely necessary
The colour of the target's logo
The number of employees at the acquirer
The age of the target business
questions.why: Acquisition buys speed at high cost and high risk. If the same capability could be built internally and there is time to do so, the organic route is usually safer. Making that comparison is what a strong evaluation does.
